passages.text: WATER, a transparent fluid, without colour, taste, or smell, which becomes solid by cold, and is raised into vapour by heat.
Water was long held by philosophers to be one of the four elements, simple and unchangeable, of which all other bodies are composed.

But Mr Cavendish and M. Lavoisier have shown, by burning inflammable air with vital air in close vessels, that water is produced, and that it is composed of these two airs; and M. Lavoisier has also decomposed it, by passing its steam through a red-hot iron tube.

According to M. Lavoisier, 100 parts of water contain about 85 parts of vital air and 15 of inflammable air, by weight. Some chemists, however, and among them Dr Priestley, still dispute this doctrine.

Water expands in freezing, so that ice is lighter than water and floats upon it; and water is found to be densest at about the fortieth degree of Fahrenheit's thermometer, a little above the freezing point.
When water is turned into vapour it absorbs a great quantity of heat, which becomes latent; and vapour is water united with caloric.

It was formerly believed that water, by long and repeated distillation, is converted into earth; but M. Lavoisier showed in 1770 that this earth comes from the glass vessels, which are worn by the water.

Water is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula H2O. It is a transparent, tasteless, odorless and nearly colorless substance, and it is the main part of Earth's oceans and of the fluids of living things.
Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms joined by covalent bonds to one oxygen atom. The molecule is polar, and hydrogen bonds between molecules give water many of its unusual properties.
Henry Cavendish showed around 1781 that water forms when hydrogen burns. Antoine Lavoisier repeated the work, named hydrogen, and showed that water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
By mass, water is about 89 percent oxygen and 11 percent hydrogen.
Water is densest at about 4 C. It expands when it freezes, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.
Water has a high heat of vaporization. Turning liquid water into steam takes a large amount of energy, which is released again when the steam condenses.
Water covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, mostly in seas and oceans.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: Cavendish, Lavoisier, composition from two gases, ice floats, densest above freezing.
Properties of water scores well but leaves out the history of the discovery.

alignments.label: A simple element

britannica.quote: one of the four elements, simple and unchangeable

wikipedia.quote: two hydrogen atoms joined by covalent bonds to one oxygen atom

alignments.note: Water is a compound, not an element. The 1797 entry reports this old view and rejects it in the next passage.

alignments.label: Two airs

britannica.quote: burning inflammable air with vital air in close vessels

wikipedia.quote: water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen

alignments.note: Same fact. Inflammable air is now hydrogen and vital air is oxygen: a change in language.

alignments.label: Proportions by weight

britannica.quote: about 85 parts of vital air and 15 of inflammable air, by weight

wikipedia.quote: about 89 percent oxygen and 11 percent hydrogen

alignments.note: The order is right: most of the weight is oxygen. Lavoisier's measurement gave too much hydrogen.

alignments.label: Still disputed

wikipedia.quote: showed that water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen

alignments.note: True in 1797, when Priestley still held to phlogiston. The dispute ended soon after, and the compound view is now settled.

britannica.quote: Water expands in freezing, so that ice is lighter than water and floats upon it

alignments.label: Greatest density

britannica.quote: densest at about the fortieth degree of Fahrenheit's thermometer

wikipedia.quote: Water is densest at about 4 C

alignments.note: Same fact in another scale. 40 F is about 4.4 C.

alignments.label: Latent heat and caloric

britannica.quote: vapour is water united with caloric

wikipedia.quote: Turning liquid water into steam takes a large amount of energy

alignments.note: Right that vapour takes in much heat. Heat is energy, not a substance called caloric that joins the water.

alignments.label: Water into earth

britannica.quote: this earth comes from the glass vessels

alignments.note: The entry reports the old belief and Lavoisier's proof against it. Wikipedia does not discuss this old belief.

alignments.label: A polar molecule
alignments.note: The 1797 entry has no idea of molecules or bonds. The formula H2O came with atomic theory in the next century.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1797 entry say water is made of?
Did chemists in 1797 agree that water is a compound?
Which 1797 facts about ice and vapour still hold?

What did the 1797 entry say water is mad.answer: It said Cavendish and Lavoisier had shown that water is made of inflammable air and vital air [B3], about 85 parts vital air to 15 inflammable air by weight [B4]. Wikipedia names these gases hydrogen and oxygen [W3] and gives about 89 percent oxygen and 11 percent hydrogen by mass [W4].

Did chemists in 1797 agree that water is.answer: Not all of them. The 1797 entry says some chemists, among them Priestley, still disputed it [B4]. Older chemists had held water to be a simple element [B2]. Wikipedia treats the compound view as settled [W3].

Which 1797 facts about ice and vapour st.answer: Water expands when it freezes, so ice floats [B5] [W5]. It is densest a little above freezing, near 40 F or 4 C [B5] [W5]. Vapour takes in a great quantity of heat [B6], which Wikipedia calls a high heat of vaporization [W6]. The 1797 idea of caloric did not hold.
